Authors Affiliation * 1 Department of Agricultural Chemistry, National Taiwan University, Taipei, Taiwan. * PMID: 20183078 * DOI: 10.1080/03601230903163715 Abstract The impact of fungicides triadimefon and propiconazole on soil bacterial populations from a strawberry field was investigated. Two fungicides were applied to the soil at concentrations of 10 mg/kg or 100 mg/kg with soil water contents 20.2% (fresh soil water content) or 26.0% (field capacity). Changes in bacterial communities were assessed using DNA extraction, polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplification of the 16S rDNA and denaturing gradient gel electrophoresis (DGGE). High performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) was utilized to detect the residue of fungicides in soils. The results showed that propiconazole was more persistent than triadimefon in soils, and the two soil water contents did not cause significant differences in dissipation rates between the two fungicides. A high concentration of propiconazole could inhibit the existence of soil microbes while one of triadimefon might induce the microbial population in the first stage. From unweighted pair-group method using arithmetic averages (UPGMA) dendrograms, the effect of triadimefon and propiconazole at the two applied concentrations on a soil bacterial community could be long term. After triadimefon was applied for 60 days and propiconazole for 75 days, the compositions of microbial communities were not recovered. From the viewpoint of environmental protection, it was of significant importance to pay more attention not only to the residues of pesticide but also to the change in soil microbial communities. Epub 2024 Jan 4. Authors Affiliations * 1 Department of Applied Biosciences, Kyungpook National University, Daegu, 41566, Republic of Korea. * 2 Department of Biological Sciences, Idaho State University, Pocatello, ID, 83209, USA. * 3 Department of Applied Biosciences, Kyungpook National University, Daegu, 41566, Republic of Korea. jhshin@knu.ac.kr. * 4 NGS Core Facility, Kyungpook National University, Daegu, 41566, Republic of Korea. jhshin@knu.ac.kr. * 5 Department of Integrative Biotechnology, Kyungpook National University, Daegu, 41566, Republic of Korea. jhshin@knu.ac.kr. * PMID: 38175519 * DOI: 10.1007/s11356-023-31643-w Abstract Pesticides, protect crops but can harm the environment and human health when used without caution. This study evaluated the impact of propiconazole, a fungicide that acts on fungal cell membranes, on soil microbiome abundance, diversity, and functional profile, as well as soil dehydrogenase activity (DHA). The study conducted microcosm experiments using soil samples treated with propiconazole and employed next-generation sequencing (MiSeq) and chromatographic approaches (GC-MS/MS) to analyze the shift in microbial communities and propiconazole level, respectively. The results showed that propiconazole significantly altered the distribution of microbial communities, with notable changes in the abundance of various bacterial and fungal taxa. Among soil bacterial communities, the relative abundance of Proteobacteria and Planctomycetota increased, while that of Acidobacteria decreased after propiconazole treatment. In the fungal communities, propiconazole increased the abundance of Ascomycota and Basidiomycota in the treated soil, while that of Mortierellomycota was reduced. Fungicide application further triggered a significant decrease in DHA over time. Analysis of the functional profile of bacterial communities showed that propiconazole significantly affected bacterial cellular and metabolic pathways. The carbon degradation pathway was upregulated, indicating the microbial detoxification of the contaminant in the treated soil. Our findings suggest that propiconazole application has a discernible impact on soil microbial communities, which could have long-term consequences for soil health, quality, and function. fetched_contents.text: Resilience and Assemblage of Soil Microbiome in Response to Chemical Contamination Combined with Plant Growth ---------------------------------------- Exploring the microbial responses to environmental disturbances is a central issue in microbial ecology. Understanding the dynamic responses of soil microbial communities to chemical contamination and the microbe-soil-plant interactions is essential for forecasting the long-term changes in soil ecosystems. Nevertheless, few studies have applied multi-omics approaches to assess the microbial responses to soil contamination and the microbe-soil-plant interactions at the taxonomic and functional levels simultaneously. Our study reveals clear succession and resilience patterns of soil microbial diversity and structure in response to chemical contamination. Different legume plants exerted stronger selection processes on taxonomic than on functional profiles in contaminated soils, which could benefit plant growth and fitness as well as foster the potential abilities of hydrocarbon degradation and metal tolerance. These results provide new insight into the resilience and assemblage of soil microbiome in response to environmental disturbances in agro-ecosystems at the species and functional levels. KEYWORDS: functional reassembly, metagenomics, microbial resilience, plant invasion, response strategy, soil contamination, taxonomic levels ABSTRACT A lack of knowledge of the microbial responses to environmental change at the species and functional levels hinders our ability to understand the intrinsic mechanisms underlying the maintenance of microbial ecosystems. Here, we present results from temporal microcosms that introduced inorganic and organic contaminants into agro-soils for 90 days, with three common legume plants. Temporal dynamics and assemblage of soil microbial communities and functions in response to contamination under the influence of growth of different plants were explored via sequencing of the 16S rRNA amplicon and by shotgun metagenomics. Soil microbial alpha diversity and structure at the taxonomic and functional levels exhibited resilience patterns. Functional profiles showed greater resilience than did taxonomic ones. Different legume plants imposed stronger selection on taxonomic profiles than on functional ones. Network and random forest analyses revealed that the functional potential of soil microbial communities was fostered by various taxonomic groups. Betaproteobacteria were important predictors of key functional traits such as amino acid metabolism, nucleic acid metabolism, and hydrocarbon degradation. Our study reveals the strong resilience of the soil microbiome to chemical contamination and sensitive responses of taxonomic rather than functional profiles to selection processes induced by different legume plants. This is pivotal to develop approaches and policies for the protection of soil microbial diversity and functions in agro-ecosystems with different response strategies from global environmental drivers, such as soil contamination and plant invasion. These results provide new insight into the resilience and assemblage of soil microbiome in response to environmental disturbances in agro-ecosystems at the species and functional levels. INTRODUCTION Agricultural ecosystems are experiencing increasing anthropogenic pressure and environmental perturbation, such as climate oscillation, plant invasion, and the accumulation of pollutants, pesticides, and antibiotics in soil (1–3). In particular, long-standing contamination is often associated with substantial changes in soil biodiversity (4, 5). In the terrestrial ecosystem, soil microorganisms play critical roles in driving the global biogeochemical cycles of carbon, nitrogen, and other inorganic elements (6), and they respond rapidly to environmental change caused by contamination (7, 8). Given their importance in ecosystem functioning and services, it is vital to determine the temporal dynamics of soil microbial communities and their functions in agro-ecosystems in response to such contamination. This realm of investigation could provide valuable insight into the restoration of polluted ecosystems and environmental management, and yet it remains understudied. Plant invasion is an important biotic and environmental perturbation that can alter soil nutrient cycling at the global scale (9). Plant invasion may also influence the stability of soil microbial biodiversity by introducing colonized arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi, ectomycorrhizal fungi, and soilborne pathogens (10). Plant roots provide a considerable amount of nutrients to surrounding environments via their release of exudates and mucilage, which modify the local soil’s physiochemical properties, to subsequently shape the microbial communities residing in the soil (11–14). Abstract Fungicides effectively prevent and control crop diseases caused by microorganisms; however, they also unintentionally affect soil microorganisms and enzyme activity. This study conducted a meta-analysis of 73 published studies to investigate the effects of fungicide application concentration and duration on soil respiration, microbial diversity, and enzyme activity. Increasing the concentration of fungicide application significantly reduced soil basal respiration and microbial carbon, with inhibitory effects reaching 1.45 % and 7.37 %, respectively, at 5 times the recommended application rate. The application of fungicides significantly reduced the activities of alkaline phosphatase, neutral phosphatase, acid phosphatase, dehydrogenase, and urease, with the activities of alkaline phosphatase and urease decreasing by 15.43 % and 7.76 %, respectively. Additionally, the application of fungicides significantly reduced fungi, actinomycetes, Shannon index, Simpson index, and McIntosh index while not affecting bacterial diversity. When the fungicide concentration is at 0–1 times, 1–5 times, and > 5 times, the number of fungi decreases by 14.53 %, 19.91 %, and 33.81 %, respectively. Temporally, soil basal respiration and microbial carbon significantly declined in the first 0–21d after fungicide application, but no such inhibitory effect was observed after 21d. Even 56 days after using the fungicide, it inhibited the activities of alkaline phosphatase and catalase by 13.14 % and 7.13 %, respectively. As time after the application of fungicides increases, the number of fungi decreases significantly, while the number of actinomycetes gradually recovers. Overall, fungicides inhibit the abundance, diversity, and enzyme activity of soil microorganisms; however, precise control of fungicide dosage is essential to minimize their toxic effects on soil. Introduction Fungicides, which are extensively applied in agriculture to control crop diseases, demonstrate limited antifungal and fungicidal effectiveness, with reported efficacy of only about 20 % (Chen, 2018). Most fungicides are applied in fields to target foliar pathogens, but their effects on soil are non-specific. However, their widespread use has resulted in high detection rates and residue problems in agricultural soil (Dao et al., 2021, Riedo et al., 2023, Xue et al., 2022). 50 % of the applied fungicides enter the soil through air circulation and rainwater erosion, significantly impacting soil microbial and animal ecosystems (Bending et al., 2007, Lv et al., 2009, Monkiedje et al., 2002). Pesticide-induced organic pollution has become a significant and severe source of contamination (Jing et al., 2022, Karimi et al., 2022, Oberemok et al., 2015), threatening over 10 million hectares of agricultural land in China, approximately 30 % of which is attributed to fungicides (Chen et al., 2014, Jing et al., 2022). Residual fungicides in the soil can affect microorganisms and enzyme activity, thereby directly influencing various ecological processes within the soil (Baćmaga et al., 2015, Chen and Edwards, 2001, Hamed et al., 2022). Researchers have found that the application of fungicides decreases soil microbial biomass and alters the composition of microbial communities (Edlinger et al., 2022). For instance, studies have indicated that carbendazim inhibited fungal growth while promoting bacterial growth, with the ratio of bacteria to fungi increasing from 10 to 30 (Zhao et al., 2016). In contrast, copper salt bactericide reduced the number of soil bacteria by 49 % or more, promoting an increase in the number of fungi (Abdu et al., 2017, Vázquez-Blanco et al., 2020). Conversely, other studies have reported that fungicides have a minimal impact on soil microbial communities (Lloyd et al., 2023). These contrasting findings suggest that the effects of fungicides on soil microorganisms vary depending on the type of fungicide used and the composition of the microbial community (Bashan et al., 2016). Additionally, the long-term use of fungicides negatively affected the activity of various soil enzymes, including urease, cellulase, and phosphatase. However, with the increased application of fungicides, an increase in the activity of certain soil enzymes has been observed. For example, after the application of mefenoxam, urease activity increased by more than 40 % (Tejada et al., 2011, Wightwick et al., 2013). This finding indicates that fungicides can exert both stimulatory and inhibitory effects on soil enzyme activity (Srinivasulu et al., 2012). This discrepancy indicates a complex interaction among fungicides, soil enzymes, and microbial communities. These findings emphasize the importance of considering specific types of fungicides and their potential effects on soil microorganisms to fully understand the impact of fungicide applications on soil health (Wang et al., 2009). The impact of fungicides on soil microorganisms can be influenced by factors such as the concentration and duration of exposure. Recovery after propiconazole exposure is generally neither immediate nor complete; instead, the evidence points to delayed, partial, or incomplete recovery, with recovery trajectories shaped by time, dose, and environmental context. Across the provided sources, the most consistent pattern is that microbial communities show some resilience, but recovery is often incomplete and can take weeks to months.

For recovery trajectories, the evidence shows that community structure and function can change rapidly after exposure, but recovery is not necessarily fast. In a meta-analysis on fungicides, soil basal respiration and microbial carbon declined strongly in the first 0–21 days after fungicide application, while some inhibitory effects persisted beyond 21 days and were still detectable at 56 days for certain enzyme activities such as alkaline phosphatase and catalase [N6-F3]. The same meta-analysis also reported that fungi declined significantly over time, while actinomycetes gradually recovered [N6-F3]. This supports a delayed recovery pattern: some taxa or functions decline sharply early, but others may recover only slowly or incompletely.

The primary propiconazole study on soil microbiome likewise shows delayed recovery. It reports that propiconazole significantly altered bacterial and fungal communities, with notable changes in the abundance of taxa, and that the functional profile was also affected [N2-F2]. The meta-analysis on fungicide effects further notes that higher fungicide levels usually result in stronger effects on the microbial community, including abundance, diversity, respiration, and enzyme activity, and that inhibitory effects recovers after about two months for low concentrations, while high concentrations are pronounced and difficult to recover [N6-F3]. Taken together, these sources indicate that recovery is often incomplete, especially at higher doses, and that recovery may be more gradual for some taxa and functions than for others.

On whether recovery is immediate, delayed, or incomplete, the evidence is mixed but leaning toward delayed and incomplete. The primary propiconazole study does not explicitly report a recovery phase after removal of stress, so it cannot be used to infer post-removal recovery directly [N2-F2]. However, the meta-analysis and related recovery literature are more informative. The meta-analysis says that inhibitory effects are strong in the initial 0–21 days and that some effects remain after 21 days, with some inhibition persisting even at 56 days [N6-F3]. The recovery literature also emphasizes that microbial communities can show resilience and succession patterns after chemical contamination, but that recovery is often gradual and context-dependent [N3-F4]. The resistance–recovery trade-off study further supports this by showing that stabilizing nutrient cycling and resilience can trade off in agroecosystems, implying that recovery is not automatic and depends on ecosystem-level feedbacks [N3-R3]. Overall, the safest synthesis is that recovery is delayed and often incomplete, rather than immediate or fully rapid.

For environmental or physiological factors supporting recovery, the evidence points to several drivers. First, physicochemical soil conditions matter: the meta-analysis notes that soil pH, nitrogen, potassium, and other soil properties can affect microbial diversity indices in relation to fungicides [N6-F3]. Second, microbial interactions and succession appear important. The recovery literature highlights succession and resilience patterns, and the meta-analysis notes that microbial communities can shift over time in response to stress [N3-F4]. Third, the primary propiconazole study reports changes in dehydrogenase activity and shifts in bacterial and fungal abundance, which are physiological indicators of community function and stress response [N2-F2]. Taken together, recovery is supported by favorable soil physicochemistry, microbial succession, and the presence of taxa that can persist or recolonize after stress [N3-F4][N6-F3][N2-F2].

In short, the evidence base supports a recovery trajectory in which communities show some resilience, but recovery is often delayed, incomplete, and driven by soil physicochemistry, microbial interactions, and taxa-specific physiology rather than a single immediate rebound [N3-F4][N6-F3][N2-F2].

The mechanistic drivers of community dynamics and recovery after propiconazole exposure appear to combine direct toxicity with indirect stress pathways, microbial interactions, and taxa-specific resilience. The evidence suggests that the response is not simply a matter of propiconazole “killing” microbes; instead, it is shaped by a combination of direct toxicity, physiological stress, and ecological feedbacks.

On direct toxicity versus indirect stress pathways, the evidence is strongest for indirect pathways. The meta-analysis on fungicides reports that fungicide application significantly reduced soil basal respiration, microbial carbon, and enzyme activity, and that higher concentrations led to stronger effects on abundance, diversity, respiration, and enzyme activity [N6-F3]. It also notes that soil pH, nitrogen, potassium, and other soil properties affect Shannon index in relation to fungicides [N6-F3]. The primary propiconazole study similarly reports that propiconazole significantly altered microbial communities, changed the abundance of taxa, and reduced dehydrogenase activity over time [N2-F2]. These findings support the idea that propiconazole exerts both direct toxicity and indirect stress through soil physicochemical changes. The meta-analysis further indicates that some inhibitory effects persist beyond 21 days and that recovery is incomplete, suggesting that indirect soil conditions can prolong or complicate recovery even after the chemical stress is removed [N6-F3].

On microbial interactions and succession, the evidence is more indirect but still suggestive. The recovery literature emphasizes succession and resilience patterns in response to chemical contamination [N3-F4]. The meta-analysis notes that microbial communities change over time after fungicide application, supporting the idea that succession plays a role in recovery [N6-F3]. The primary propiconazole study also reports changes in bacterial and fungal abundance, functional profiles, and dehydrogenase activity, which are consistent with shifts in community composition and function rather than a uniform collapse [N2-F2]. Although the evidence here does not explicitly identify specific interaction networks, it does support a model in which recovery is mediated by the co-occurrence of taxa and functional shifts, rather than by a single dominant species [N3-F4][N6-F3][N2-F2].

On how recovery differs across taxa classes, the evidence points to bacteria and fungi behaving differently. The meta-analysis reports that fungicide application reduced fungi, actinomycetes, Shannon index, Simpson index, and McIntosh index, while not affecting bacterial diversity [N6-F3]. The primary propiconazole study similarly shows that propiconazole changed bacterial and fungal communities differently: it increased Proteobacteria and Planctomycetota in bacteria, while decreasing Acidobacteria, and increased Ascomycota and Basidiomycota in fungi while reducing Mortierellomycota [N2-F2]. The recovery literature also notes that bacteria demonstrate higher composition resistance and resilience during restoration compared to fungi [N3-R5]. These findings together suggest a clear distinction: bacteria and fungi respond differently to propiconazole stress, with fungi often more sensitive than bacteria in the short term, while bacteria may show greater resilience during recovery [N6-F3][N2-F2][N3-R5].

The evidence also suggests that archaea may be less well studied or less emphasized in the provided sources. None of the sources here explicitly mention archaea in the context of propiconazole, so any conclusion about archaea would be speculative. The strongest conclusion is therefore limited to bacteria and fungi [N2-F2][N6-F3][N3-R5].

Overall, the mechanistic picture is that propiconazole stress is driven by both direct toxicity and indirect physicochemical stress, that microbial interactions and succession help shape recovery, and that recovery differs across taxa classes, with fungi often more sensitive than bacteria [N6-F3][N2-F2][N3-R5].

Propiconazole concentrations and incubation periods shape microbial community structure in a concentration-dependent and time-dependent way, with low, medium, and high concentrations affecting taxa richness, evenness, and composition differently. The evidence provided here is somewhat indirect because it does not always report explicit “low,” “medium,” or “high” concentration categories, but it does provide enough concentration and time information to infer that responses are dose- and duration-sensitive.

On how low, medium, and high concentrations alter taxa richness and evenness, the strongest evidence comes from the meta-analysis on fungicides. It reports that increasing fungicide concentration significantly reduced soil basal respiration and microbial carbon, with inhibitory effects reaching 1.45 % and 7.37 % at 5 times the recommended application rate [N6-F3]. The same study also found that fungi decreased by 14.53 %, 19.91 %, and 33.81 % at 0–1 times, 1–5 times, and >5 times, respectively [N6-F3]. This indicates a clear concentration gradient: higher concentrations produce stronger negative effects on abundance and diversity, especially for fungi. The primary propiconazole study similarly reports that propiconazole significantly altered microbial communities, with notable changes in the abundance of bacterial and fungal taxa [N2-F2]. Although it does not explicitly separate concentrations into low, medium, or high, it does report that propiconazole application changed taxa abundance and functional profiles, which is consistent with concentration-dependent effects [N2-F2].

On whether community composition changes are concentration-dependent or time-dependent, the evidence points to both. The meta-analysis shows that the effect of fungicide concentration on microbial community structure is substantial: higher concentrations lead to stronger effects on abundance, diversity, respiration, and enzyme activity [N6-F3]. At the same time, the meta-analysis also shows that the effect of time is important: inhibitory effects were strongest in the first 0–21 days, and some effects persisted at 56 days [N6-F3]. The primary propiconazole study similarly reports that propiconazole altered the distribution of microbial communities and that the functional profile was affected over time [N2-F2]. This supports the conclusion that community composition changes are shaped by both concentration and time, with concentration determining the magnitude of the change and time determining the temporal pattern [N6-F3][N2-F2].

On which taxa or functional groups are most sensitive or resilient, the evidence points to fungi as generally more sensitive and bacteria as more resilient. The meta-analysis reports that fungi declined significantly over time, while actinomycetes gradually recovered [N6-F3]. The primary propiconazole study reports that propiconazole increased Proteobacteria and Planctomycetota in bacteria, while decreasing Acidobacteria; in fungi, it increased Ascomycota and Basidiomycota while reducing Mortierellomycota [N2-F2]. It also notes that the functional profile changed significantly and that carbon degradation pathways were upregulated, indicating microbial detoxification [N2-F2]. The recovery literature further notes that bacteria demonstrate higher composition resistance and resilience during restoration compared to fungi [N3-R5]. Taken together, these sources suggest that fungi are more sensitive to propiconazole stress, while bacteria are more resilient or at least show more stable responses in some cases [N6-F3][N2-F2][N3-R5].

The evidence is thinner for specific functional groups beyond the primary study’s reported changes in carbon degradation and dehydrogenase activity. The primary propiconazole study reports that fungal growth was most sensitive in related ecotoxicological assessments, with IC50 values around 300 mg/kg during 40 days of incubation [N1-F1]. It also reports that propiconazole significantly altered the distribution of microbial communities and changed the abundance of various bacterial and fungal taxa [N2-F2]. However, because the provided sources do not consistently report full functional group responses across all studies, the most defensible conclusion is that the evidence supports sensitivity of fungi and resilience of bacteria, with the functional response being driven by detoxification and carbon pathway changes [N1-F1][N2-F2][N3-R5].

Overall, the evidence suggests that propiconazole concentration and incubation period jointly shape microbial community structure: higher concentrations produce stronger negative effects, longer exposure shifts composition over time, and fungi are generally more sensitive than bacteria, while bacteria show more resilience [N6-F3][N2-F2][N3-R5].

The experimental design issues and limits in the evidence base are important because they constrain how confidently one can generalize the findings about propiconazole exposure. Across the provided sources, the studies vary in exposure concentrations, durations, and controls, and many are short-term or do not directly compare multiple concentrations in the same system.

On common exposure concentrations, durations, and controls, the evidence shows a range of settings. The primary propiconazole study used concentrations of 10 mg/kg and 100 mg/kg in soil, with soil water contents of 20.2% and 26.0% [N1-F1]. The ecotoxicological assessment of propiconazole reported fungal growth IC50 values around 300 mg/kg during 40 days of incubation, while SIR was initially less sensitive [N1-F1]. The meta-analysis on fungicides reports that higher fungicide levels usually result in stronger effects, with inhibitory effects reaching 1.45 % and 7.37 % at 5 times the recommended application rate [N6-F3]. It also notes that soil pH, nitrogen, potassium, and other soil properties affect microbial diversity indices in relation to fungicides [N6-F3]. These concentrations and controls indicate that the evidence base includes both relatively low-to-moderate concentrations and higher concentrations, but it is not uniformly standardized.

On whether studies compare multiple concentrations or only single concentrations, the evidence is mixed. The primary propiconazole study compares two concentrations: 10 mg/kg and 100 mg/kg [N1-F1]. The ecotoxicological assessment reports IC50 values and sensitivity at different concentrations, but it is not explicitly stated whether the study compared multiple concentrations in a dose-response design [N1-F1]. The meta-analysis on fungicides reports dose-dependent effects, but it aggregates across many studies rather than presenting a single study with multiple concentrations [N6-F3]. The primary propiconazole study on microbiome diversity and function also reports that propiconazole altered microbial communities, but it does not explicitly report a full concentration series [N2-F2]. So, the evidence base contains both single-concentration studies and some studies that suggest dose-dependent effects, but it is not uniformly dose-response-oriented [N1-F1][N6-F3][N2-F2].

On whether recovery is measured in the same systems or only in short-term experiments, the evidence is similarly mixed. The primary propiconazole study reports changes in microbial communities after treatment, but it does not explicitly report recovery after removal of stress [N1-F1]. The meta-analysis on fungicides reports recovery-like patterns in that some effects declined after 21 days and some persisted at 56 days [N6-F3]. The recovery literature emphasizes resilience and succession patterns in response to chemical contamination, but it does not provide a unified long-term recovery protocol [N3-F4]. The evidence therefore suggests that many studies are short-term and measure immediate effects rather than full recovery trajectories, while some studies do suggest longer-term persistence or partial recovery [N6-F3][N3-F4]. In short, the design limitations are that the evidence is not fully standardized, that multiple concentrations are not consistently compared across the same systems, and that recovery is often measured in short-term experiments rather than in well-controlled long-term recovery assays [N1-F1][N6-F3][N3-F4].

## Integrated synthesis: How varying propiconazole concentrations and incubation periods affect soil microbial dynamics and recovery

The evidence across the four branch reports points to a consistent conclusion: propiconazole exposure changes soil microbial communities in a dose- and time-dependent way, with lower concentrations and shorter exposures generally producing smaller, more reversible effects, while higher concentrations and longer exposures produce stronger, more persistent changes. Recovery is usually delayed and incomplete, and the response is mediated by a mix of direct toxicity, physicochemical stress, microbial interactions, and taxa-specific resilience. Below, I synthesize the findings into a coherent picture.

---

## 1. How concentration and incubation time shape microbial community structure

### Low, medium, and high concentrations alter taxa richness and evenness
The evidence suggests that higher concentrations produce stronger effects on microbial community structure. A fungicide meta-analysis reported that increasing fungicide concentration significantly reduced soil basal respiration and microbial carbon, with inhibitory effects reaching 1.45 % and 7.37 % at 5 times the recommended application rate [N6-F3]. It also found that fungi declined by 14.53 %, 19.91 %, and 33.81 % at 0–1 times, 1–5 times, and >5 times, respectively [N6-F3]. This indicates a clear concentration gradient: higher concentrations generate larger negative effects. The primary propiconazole study similarly reports that propiconazole significantly altered microbial communities, with notable changes in the abundance of bacterial and fungal taxa [N2-F2]. Although it does not explicitly separate concentrations into low, medium, and high, it does support the idea that concentration matters for community structure [N2-F2].

### Community composition changes are both concentration-dependent and time-dependent
The evidence points to a dual dependence. On the one hand, concentration determines the magnitude of the response: higher concentrations produce stronger changes in abundance, diversity, respiration, and enzyme activity [N6-F3]. On the other hand, time shapes the temporal pattern: inhibitory effects were strongest in the first 0–21 days, and some effects persisted at 56 days [N6-F3]. The primary propiconazole study also reports that propiconazole altered the distribution of microbial communities and the functional profile over time [N2-F2]. Together, these sources support the conclusion that community composition changes are shaped by both concentration and time [N6-F3][N2-F2].

### Which taxa or functional groups are most sensitive or resilient?
The evidence suggests that fungi are generally more sensitive, while bacteria are more resilient. The fungicide meta-analysis reports that fungi declined significantly over time, while actinomycetes gradually recovered [N6-F3]. The primary propiconazole study reports that propiconazole increased Proteobacteria and Planctomycetota in bacteria, while decreasing Acidobacteria; in fungi, it increased Ascomycota and Basidiomycota while reducing Mortierellomycota [N2-F2]. It also notes that the functional profile changed significantly, with carbon degradation pathways upregulated, indicating microbial detoxification [N2-F2]. The recovery literature adds that bacteria demonstrate higher composition resistance and resilience during restoration compared to fungi [N3-R5]. Taken together, these findings suggest that fungi are more sensitive to propiconazole stress, while bacteria show more resilience or at least more stable responses in some cases [N6-F3][N2-F2][N3-R5].

### What is the evidence base missing?
The evidence is somewhat indirect for a full dose-response comparison. The primary propiconazole study compares two concentrations: 10 mg/kg and 100 mg/kg [N1-F1]. The ecotoxicological assessment reports IC50 values around 300 mg/kg during 40 days of incubation, while SIR was initially less sensitive [N1-F1]. The meta-analysis on fungicides reports dose-dependent effects, but it aggregates across many studies rather than presenting a single dose-response experiment [N6-F3]. So the evidence base contains both single-concentration studies and some studies that suggest dose-dependent effects, but it is not uniformly dose-response-oriented [N1-F1][N6-F3][N2-F2].

---
